score_evidence: 'They said it couldn't be done, but we created the world's first-ever Bluetooth connection to space.' → lab_language_intensity (first-ever demo framing as the headline proof point)
'Satellite connectivity is coming soon' / '* Satellite network coming soon.' → lab_language_intensity (the capability a DoD user would buy is not yet delivered)

'All data is end-to-end encrypted using industry-standard AES encryption, from device to destination.' → deployment_awareness_absence (AES named as the security story; zero mention of FIPS 140-3, ATO/RMF, STIG, IL4/IL5, CMMC, or ITAR across ~1441 words)

'Purpose-built for industries that rely on timely visibility into asset location and condition' with use cases 'Cold Chain Monitoring / Rental Equipment Recovery / Warehouse & Yard Visibility' → operator_absence (audience is enterprise logistics; no operator, warfighter, CONOPS, or training language anywhere)

'Hubble Network Raises $70M Series B to Scale Global Bluetooth-to-Satellite Connectivity' (2025-09-17) → stage_pressure scored low; capital runway removes near-term existential clock

blind_spots.blind_spot: The 'global' terrestrial network is a consumer-phone gateway mesh, which does not exist where DoD operates
blind_spots.operator_reality: Coverage is generated by 100M+ third-party Bluetooth scanning access points — overwhelmingly civilian smartphones and consumer devices in cities. At an austere OCONUS site or in a contested littoral there is no such gateway population, so a tag that reports flawlessly in a Seattle warehouse goes silent the moment it matters. This is the same failure class as the 30fps crowd-detection case: the architecture silently assumes an infrastructure the deployed environment does not supply.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: The company's live revenue is commercial logistics, where dense civilian gateway coverage is a feature, not an assumption to be tested. Nobody on the team is hired to model coverage in a denied theater.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Bluetooth signals are transmitted over a network of 100M+ access points, delivering indoor, urban, and in-transit visibility across continents.

blind_spots.blind_spot: AES is presented as the security architecture, with no path to an ATO for the dashboard that delivers the data
blind_spots.operator_reality: The product's value is delivered through a cloud management dashboard. On the government side that dashboard is the thing that needs IL4/IL5 hosting, STIG-hardened components, FIPS 140-3 validated crypto modules (not merely 'industry-standard AES'), a POA&M, and an ISSO to shepherd RMF. Months-to-ATO is the schedule item that eats the funded period of performance, and none of it appears in their language or their hiring.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Enterprise buyers accept 'AES end-to-end' as sufficient. No compliance, security-engineering, or ISSO role appears in the open-roles list to raise the question internally.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: All data is end-to-end encrypted using industry-standard AES encryption, from device to destination.

blind_spots.blind_spot: A 'hard-to-detect' 2.4 GHz emitter on a government asset is an EMCON and ITAR problem, not just a stealth feature
blind_spots.operator_reality: Their covert-tracking pitch treats detectability purely as an anti-theft concern — hiding from a car thief. On a military platform the adversary is doing RF direction-finding, so a periodic 4 dBm 2.4 GHz beacon is a signature that can geolocate the asset it is protecting, and the location history itself becomes controlled data under ITAR/export rules once it transits a commercial network and a commercial cloud. Nothing in their material distinguishes 'not easily discoverable by a thief' from 'survivable against an EW-capable adversary'.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Their threat model is written for stolen-vehicle recovery and rental-equipment loss, where the opposing force has no SIGINT capability.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Each device communicates via a proprietary 2.4 GHz protocol, allowing it to be tracked by Hubble without being easily discoverable.

opener_hook: Hubble holds an Air Force STTR for 'Bluetooth to Space' (FA8649-, $109,998, 2024), but the network live today is 100M+ consumer scanning gateways — a population that doesn't exist at the OCONUS sites that award is aimed at.
what_they_do: Runs a global low-bandwidth connectivity network that any off-the-shelf Bluetooth chip can reach — today via 100M+ terrestrial scanning gateways, with a satellite constellation in progress — for asset, vehicle, and cargo tracking.
